Everything you need to know about introducing this juicy fruit to your little one.\n\nPineapple is irresistibly sweet (just like your little sweetie), so chances are you won’t have to work too hard at encouraging him to gobble the tropical fruit up. Better still, pineapple can be a perfect early finger food, whether you’re starting off with baby-led weaning or moving on from purées. Here’s the scoop on serving pineapple to babies and toddlers.\n\nWhen can babies have pineapple?\n\nYou can put pineapple on the menu as soon as your baby starts solids, usually around 6 months. If you're spoon-feeding purées, you can serve the fruit in purée form at first, but if you're going the baby-led weaning route (an approach that introduces solids in the form of soft, gummable finger foods) you'll need to do a little bit of prep work to make pineapple safe for early eaters.\n\nHow to prepare pineapple for your baby\n\nPineapple can be on the firmer side, so first and foremost, be sure to cut it into age-appropriate pieces. Long strips are the way to go for new eaters. Inspect the pieces to make sure they don’t contain any of the pineapple’s hard core or spots of the tough outer peel, since both can be choking hazards.\n\nBoth fresh and thawed frozen pineapple are equally good choices for your cutie. Canned pineapple isn’t the best option for babies and toddlers, however, since it tends to contain extra sugar. If you do serve a canned variety, stick with pineapple that has been packed in its natural juices instead of syrup. Drain and rinse the fruit well to remove as much extra juice as you can and serve it in small quantities.\n\nWhat about pineapple juice? The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) says juice is not appropriate for babies under 1, who should fill up on breast milk or formula, then solid foods. It’s okay for toddlers over 1 to have small amounts (no more than 4 ounces) of 100 percent fruit juice as an occasional treat, but whole fruit remains a healthier choice.\n\nThe tips below can help parents determine how to serve pineapple at different stages, but keep in mind that all babies develop at their own pace. Speak with your pediatrician before beginning baby-led weaning, and talk to him or her if you have any concerns about your child's oral-motor skills, chewing skills, swallowing skills or if you're unsure whether or not your baby is ready for certain food preparations.\n\nHow to prepare pineapple for a 6-month-old\n\nOffer pineapple sliced into wide, thin strips — think the size of your index and middle finger together — for your baby to palm and gum. Even if he can’t quite manage to chew it, he'll love sucking the pineapple’s juices. If the pineapple is slippery, try rolling it in baby cereal to make it more grippable.\n\nHow to prepare pineapple for a 9-month-old\n\nAs long as your little one has a few teeth, you can start serving thinner, pinky-sized strips for him to pick up and bite.\n\nHow to prepare pineapple for a 12-month-old and up\n\nAt 1 year old, your new toddler may be ready to handle pineapple cut into small half-inch cubes. He can pick them up with his fingers or practice spearing them with a fork.\n\nPineapple recipes for babies and toddlers\n\nYour diner will probably happily devour sweet, juicy pineapple all by itself. But there are many ways to pack other dishes with a pineapple punch, too. Just remember to always introduce one food at a time, especially top allergens like eggs, peanuts, soy, wheat, dairy and seafood.\n\nRoasted pineapple. Bake pineapple slices in the oven or toaster until soft and caramelized. Serve plain or with a squeeze of fresh lime juice for a flavor explosion.\n\nRoasted pineapple “sundae.” Top plain yogurt with chopped roasted pineapple pieces and a cherry (pitted and quartered).\n\nTropical oatmeal. Cook oatmeal with coconut milk and top with fresh diced pineapple and mango.\n\nPineapple upside-down pancakes. Core pineapple and slice into rings. Place one ring in the middle of a whole grain pancake while the underside cooks, then flip.\n\nNutty pineapple-banana smoothie. Blend banana and pineapple chunks with plain yogurt and a spoonful of cashew butter to make a creamy drink.\n\nPineapple-chicken stir-fry. Swap out half the veggies for pineapple in your favorite chicken stir-fry recipe.\n\nPineapple fried rice. Throw in some very small cubed pineapple pieces at the same time as the veggies so the flavors have a chance to meld.\n\nWhat are the benefits of pineapple for babies and toddlers?\n\nFirst and foremost? Pineapple is packed with vitamin C, which supports immune health and enhances your tot’s absorption of iron. That makes it a tasty treat to serve alongside iron-rich foods like beef, poultry or beans.\n\nThe golden fruit is also good for bone health. (Who knew?) Pineapple is rich in manganese, a trace mineral involved in helping your baby or toddler build strong, sturdy bones.\n\nCan babies be allergic to pineapple?\n\nNotice a red rash or hive-like bumps around your little one’s mouth or hands after he eats pineapple? It could be an allergic reaction — but more likely, his skin could just be slightly irritated from the fruit’s acidity.\n\nThese types of rashes typically are not harmful, so you probably don’t need to put pineapple on the do-not-eat list if your baby doesn’t seem bothered. But it’s worth bringing it up with the pediatrician, especially if the rash seems to make your little one itchy.\n\nAnecdotally, some parents say that pineapple’s acidity seems to worsen their child's reflux or cause diaper rashes. That’s not necessarily a reason to avoid introducing the fruit. But if you notice that your baby seems uncomfortable or his diaper area is irritated after eating pineapple, consider taking a break until you can talk about his symptoms with the doctor.\n\nAs for true pineapple allergies? They aren’t common, but reactions are still possible. Raw pineapple, in particular, can trigger oral allergy syndrome — a condition caused by cross-reaction in allergens found in both pollen and raw fruits and vegetables. It’s more likely in kids over 3, but babies and toddlers can be affected.\n\nIt’s always a good idea to be on the lookout for signs of a possible allergic reaction, especially when you’re serving a food for the first time. Your baby or toddler might have a food allergy if, soon after eating (within minutes to a few hours), he experiences:\n\nHives\n\nItching\n\nSkin, lip or tongue swelling\n\nSneezing\n\nWheezing\n\nThroat tightness or trouble swallowing\n\nNausea, vomiting, stomach pain or diarrhea\n\nTrouble breathing\n\nCall your doctor right away if your child experiences symptoms of an allergic reaction. In the rare event that your child shows signs of a life-threatening allergic reaction like trouble breathing or swallowing, call 911 right away.\n\nIs pineapple a choking hazard for babies?\n\nRaw, firm fruits like pineapple can be a choking hazard for babies. Make sure you prepare pineapple safely for your little eater by serving it in an age-appropriate size, removing the hard core and skin, and always offering pineapple that is very ripe and soft.\n\nMake sure, too, to always supervise your young child when he's eating, sit him upright during mealtimes and never serve food while he's reclining, walking, sitting in a car seat or playing.\n\nPineapple can have a sweet spot on your child's menu early on.   >>     24:   "content_body": "Making Bathtime Fun for Babies and Toddlers\n\nWant to make a splash in the bath? Pump up the tub fun (but stay safe) with these age-by-age activities.\n\nAmong the nerve-wracking tasks that new parents face is a baby’s first bath. Indeed, washing a wriggly, slippery newborn is a bit tricky, but once you both get your sea legs, bath time can also be a great way to bond. Your goal is a clean cutie, of course, but for babies and toddlers, the bathtub is like a personal water park, complete with games, bubbles and toys galore.\n\nAnd the best part? Bathtime plays on endless repeat, as your child gets to come back a few times a week for yet more wet and wild adventures. To up the fun quotient, try these games and activities on your bathing beauty and see which ones float your baby's (toy) boat!\n\nTips to make bathtime more fun\n\nBathtime activities for babies\n\nChoose the best toys. There are a ton of bath toys on the market, but the top ones help a baby learn while she plays. For example, plastic cups in a variety of sizes encourage pouring, filling and dumping, while a set of floating sea creatures allows for imaginary play , language practice and counting skills.\n\nBring on the bubbles. You can blow and your child can pop; once she's a bit older you can switch jobs. A variety of wands let’s your baby explore the concepts of big and small (not to mention high and low and fast and slow). Narrate as you go, and she'll soon learn the words \"float\" and \"pop.\"\n\nMake it foamy. Add some tear-free foam soap or bubble bath to the water and you've got the makings for some excellent beards, mustaches and more!\n\nTry bath books. Yup, there are plastic-coated bath books that are ideal for reading in the water. Choose ones that match the scene, such as tales about ocean creatures, boats or mermaids.\n\nSing while sudsing. Unleash your inner songstress and sing a mashup of made-for-the-tub tunes (like \"Splish Splash\" and \"Rubber Duckie\") or your latest playlist fave. Your baby will love it — even if you're totally off-key — and you'll expand her music and language skills.\n\nAdd a mirror. A baby who’s not too keen on her bath routine might be swayed by mirror play in the water. Just make sure to choose an unbreakable one made from baby-friendly plastic or acrylic.\n\nIntroduce textures. Bathtime is a great opportunity to tickle your little one's senses with new textures, such as a bath sponge, a wet washcloth, a dry towel and shaving cream.\n\nThrow a puppet show. Got a bath mitt? Insert your hand into this little terry pocket and create a talking creature to entertain your baby.\n\nSplash — a lot! Face it, the best fun in the tub is slamming your hands, kicking your legs and shrieking to hear the echo bounce off the tile. Allow your baby to let loose (safely, of course!).\n\nBathtime activities for toddlers\n\nHit the wall. Where else can your toddler scrawl on the walls than the bathroom’s tile? Just give her the tools she needs and watch the creativity explode. Options include soap crayons, bathtub finger paints and markers, reusable stickers and foam shapes that stick when wet.\n\nFoster a fantasy. Your tub can become a pirate ship sailing the high seas or a fishing vessel trawling for the next big catch. Stories can make bathtime fascinating, so break out your best water-themed tales and encourage your little one to imagine along with you.\n\nPlay some music. Play tunes on your phone to up the jazzy feel of bath night.\n\nOffer your tub. Her bathroom is perfectly fine, but yours is divine! As a special treat, let your toddler have her shampoo in your tub.\n\nSwap in real toys. Bath toys lose their luster after a while, so consider all other plastic playthings in your child’s room for a change. Army men, plastic animals and dolls are safe in water, and most float!\n\nAdd a treat. Drippy ice pops are hard to manage at the kitchen table, but they’re ideal in the bathtub. Save dessert for this easy-clean space and wash the sugary, sticky mess down the drain.\n\nMake a race track. Use the entire tub as a play space by bringing your tot’s cars into the bathroom. Mini trucks and convertibles can vroom and zoom along the tub’s edge.\n\nJoin the fun. You probably used to share the tub with your baby, but she’s long forgotten. But the novelty of you squeezing in now will no doubt thrill your toddler. Bonus: She can wash your back and your feet while you sit back and relax.\n\nDIY bath toys to try\n\nMake a few waves by introducing bath toys your little one is sure to love. These DIY baby toys for the tub guarantee bathtime fun, plus they score high on creativity (and low on out-of-pocket expense).\n\nA rain shower. When it rains it pours — or if you make this DIY baby toy, gently showers. Use an awl (or any pointed tool) to punch a few holes in the bottom of a yogurt cup or plastic container. Then let your little one at it. As fast as she fills it up, she’ll see (and feel) the drops drizzle out the bottom — the kind of instant feedback that wows wee ones. Take a turn letting the rain drip on her noggin, then let her do the same on your hand (or your head if you're bathing with your baby).\n\nBaby-friendly water balloons. What makes for great baby bath toys? Easy-to-grasp items that most babies can manipulate. That’s why these homemade water balloons are sure to be a hit. To make these DIY bath toys, let your honey help you pour water into Ziploc plastic bags until they're three-quarters full, then seal them up and hand them over. (Real balloons are a no-no for babies, since they can break and pose a choking hazard.) She can hold them, shake them, squeeze them, or throw them back into the water — and laugh when they make a splash. For sportier fun, place a small plastic colander at the other end of the tub and show your little one how to shoot a basket.\n\nA squirt gun. Real water guns are too much for little hands to manage (and who needs guns, anyway?). Get the same effect for your little squirt with this DIY baby toy — a plastic turkey baster. Let her watch as you squeeze the bulb, plunge the tip in the water, then fill up the tube with H2O. Gently shoot at those chubby thighs and show her how to aim at other tub toys. She might even manage to use the baster to blow a few bubbles under water — a neat trick on its own and one that builds hand muscles as she squeezes. No turkey baster? A nose-bulb syringe works well too, and it’s easier for your tot to grasp. Just keep a separate one on hand to suction out your sweetie’s nostrils when she’s sick — baby bath toys tend to grow mold quickly, and you don’t want to stick a grimy bulb up her nose.\n\nA sponge boat. The most awesome thing about the bathtub? Stuff floats! Sure, that’s old news to you, but to babies it’s mesmerizing (and the best toys for babies are ones that grab their attention). One easy-to-make DIY bath toy that’s fabulously floatable: A sponge boat. Cut a slot in a new kitchen sponge, then cut another sponge into a large triangle for a sail and slip it into the slot. Now show your bathing beauty how her rubber duckie can take a cruise around the tub. (Just keep an eye out so your cutie doesn’t chomp down and tear off a chokeable mouthful.) Sponges also provide excellent squeezing opportunities, so show your water baby how to soak it up and smoosh it out. Amazing!\n\nPlaying with babies and toddlers safely in the tub\n\nYou can use a bath seat or ring if it makes you feel more comfortable, but it's no substitute for being within arm's reach during every single second of your baby's bath. Never leave your child unattended in the bath.\n\nHere’s more about water safety:\n\nGather supplies ahead of time. Be sure to arrange everything you need for bathtime before you start, including her towel and lotion. If you forget something, someone else will have to get it for you, or you’ll need to take your baby out of the tub and carry her with you to retrieve the item.\n\nCheck the temp. Keep the water temperature on target by putting the thermostat setting of your hot-water heater at 120 degrees Fahrenheit or below. And always test the water with your elbow or inner wrist before you put your baby or toddler in for her scrub-down.\n\nAdd non-skid decals. Wet, slippery surfaces are an accident waiting to happen. To help prevent falls, choose a bathroom rug with a rubber backing, apply textured decals or a shower mat to the bottom of the tub, and wrap the tub spout with a soft cover to ease the pain if your tot bumps her head on it.\n\nRemove electronics. It goes without saying, but electricity and water do not mix. Before bathtime, stash hair dryers, razors and similar devices in a locked cabinet. Even better: Keep them in a linen closet in the hallway, if you can.\n\nBathtime is the best time for babies and toddlers. They have your undivided attention in a wonderland filled with bubbles, toys and more. If you always keep safety in mind when your child is near water, your scrubs in the tubs will go off without a hitch.",

Here's the Deal\n\nby Heidi Murkoff, author of What to Expect When You're Expecting.\n\nUpdates to copy, sources, and formatting.\n\nYour aching back and other pregnancy pains might have you craving a soothing soak in a hot tub or a relaxing lounge in a sauna. But is it safe to go into a hot tub or sauna while you're pregnant?\n\nHere's what you need to know about saunas and hot tubs during pregnancy.\n\nKey Takeaways\n\nSkip hot tubs and saunas for now. They can raise your core temperature too high, which may pose risks to your developing baby — especially early on.\n\nDon’t worry if you used a hot tub before you knew you were pregnant. Most people get out long before their temperature reaches a risky level. But if you have any concerns about your exposure, talk to your provider.\n\nA warm (not hot) bath is your safest soak. It eases aches without raising your body temperature too much, so it’s perfect for a little relaxation during pregnancy.\n\nCan you get into a hot tub or sauna while you're pregnant?\n\nWhile you don't need to switch to cold showers, it's probably a good idea to skip the hot tub and the sauna when you're pregnant. While sitting in a sauna or soaking in a hot tub may seem like the perfect remedy for soothing your pregnancy aches and pains, both activities are risky.\n\nFirst of all, pregnant women are at a greater risk for dehydration, dizziness, and lower blood pressure in general, and these symptoms may intensify in extreme heat.\n\nPlus, anything that raises your core body temperature to more than 101 degrees Fahrenheit and keeps it there for a while is potentially hazardous to your baby — especially during the early months, when your little one's body and brain are developing.\n\nResearch shows that exposure to high temperatures can increase your baby’s risk of neural tube defects of the brain, spine, or spinal cord during the first month of pregnancy, including spina bifida, a birth disorder that occurs when a baby’s backbone doesn't fully close as it develops.\n\nAre hot tubs and saunas ever safe during pregnancy?\n\nAgain, you'll probably want to avoid the saunas and hot tubs completely during pregnancy until your doctor gives you the green light after you've delivered. But if you absolutely can’t resist, take these safety precautions to reduce the risk of harming your baby:\n\nMost hot tubs are set at between 100 and 102 degrees F, with 104 degrees F being the maximum temperature setting. Adjust yours to maintain a lower temperature — around 97 to 98 degrees F — and keep a thermometer in the water to make sure it stays that way.\n\nLimit soak or sauna time to less than 10 minutes.\n\nGet out of the tub as soon as you feel any discomfort, including sweating or signs of overheating like dizziness or clamminess.\n\nIf you have any chronic health conditions or pregnancy complications, or if you're already feeling warm due to exercise or fever, stay out of the tub.\n\nDip only your feet into the whirlpool's warm water, and limit the soak to less than 10 minutes at a time.\n\nWant guidance on what else to skip during pregnancy — and what’s safe? Get all your questions answered and concerns addressed in the What to Expect app.\n\nWhat if you’ve already been in a hot tub or sauna? It’s a question on the mind of many parents-to-be.\n\n“I’ve been going to the sauna and hot tub for the first 6 weeks before knowing I was pregnant,” says What to Expect Community member AgnieszkaHallab, “and now I’m freaking out.”\n\nThe reassuring news is there isn't much cause for concern. Most women get out before their body temperature reaches 101 degrees because the heat gets too uncomfortable, so it’s likely you did too.\n\nBut if you’re worried, speak with your practitioner, who may recommend an ultrasound or other prenatal test to make sure everything is on track with your baby's development.\n\nYour best bet while you’re building that baby is to stick to a warm (not hot) bath — since most of your upper body stays of the water in the tub, you’re a lot less likely to overheat. Add some bubbles and a scented candle to the mix and watch your tension go right down the drain.\n\nHere’s to a safe and healthy pregnancy!\n\nWhat to Expect When You're Expecting, 5th edition, Heidi Murkoff. The sound of water rushing down the drain may frighten her.\n\nTry, try again\n\nDon’t worry if your little one doesn’t take the bait right away. Although the odds of this happening are very slim, here's a step-by-step rundown of what you should do.\n\nAs you near your due date, you’re likely brimming with excitement — and, if you’re like many pregnant moms, also brimming with “what ifs.” Like: What if I go into labor when I’m home alone and can’t make it to the hospital?\n\nAlthough that scenario is common in soap operas, an unplanned home birth isn’t nearly as likely in real life. According to the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG), fewer than 1% of births occur in the home, and only a quarter of those are unplanned. Trusted SourceAmerican College of Obstetricians and GynecologistsPlanned Home BirthSee All Sources [1]\n\nBut to lay your fears to rest (or in the case you are that rare mom who finds herself snowed in on delivery day), here’s what you should know for an emergency labor by yourself at home:\n\n1. Assess the situation\n\nFirst things first: How do you know if the baby’s coming quickly and you won’t make it to the hospital?\n\nWhile every woman's labor is different, if you’re having strong, long, frequent contractions (generally occurring fewer than five minutes apart), and/or if your water has broken and you have a strong urge to push, you’re experiencing signs that delivery is imminent. Trusted SourceAmerican College of Obstetricians and GynecologistsHow to Tell When Labor BeginsSee All Sources [2]\n\nEvery labor is different, but on average, First babies do tend to take longer than subsequent ones — so if you’re having your second or third child, your little one may make his grand entrance a little more quickly.\n\n2. Call 911\n\nSounds obvious, but in all the excitement (baby’s on the way!) you don’t want to forget to call 911 as soon as possible. They’ll get medical professionals en route. Ask them to also call your practitioner.\n\nMost emergency dispatchers are also trained on how to talk you through the basic steps of a home birth, so if possible, put them on speaker phone. And, if you can, unlock your door so the EMTs can enter easily, as you may not be in any condition to usher them in by the time they arrive.\n\nYou’ll also want to take off your pants and underwear and try to get as comfortable as possible. Settle yourself in a semi-reclined position or, if lying down, place a rolled-up towel under your left hip. Trusted SourceNational Institutes of Health, National Library of MedicineEMS Prehospital DeliveriesSee All Sources [3] Now, breathe, long deep breaths. Reassure yourself that help is on the way.\n\n3. Stay calm and make yourself as comfortable as possible\n\nWhile an unplanned delivery at home may seem frightening, try your best to keep calm and remember: Your body knows how to do this!\n\nWash your hands and your vaginal area with soap. Grab a bucket of warm water and at least four clean towels, which you can use to wipe your baby down and keep him warm.\n\nThough your first impulse might be to lie in the tub to avoid a messy cleanup, you won’t be comfortable there — or easily accessible to the EMTs. Instead, lay clean sheets, towels, or a waterproof covering such as a plastic bag or shower curtain over your bed or on a rug on the floor.\n\nLie down, and to get more comfortable, try to prop yourself up with a bunch of pillows. In this position, you can also easily reach down with both hands and help ease your baby out.\n\nIf someone’s around to help you (i.e., you go into labor in a Walmart parking lot or are at home with your partner and can’t get to the hospital), most of the advice is the same.\n\n4. Resist the urge to push — until you can't\n\nWhen having a baby unexpectedly, it’s better not to bear down, since you could risk the baby coming out quickly and damaging your delicate tissue. Panting can help, since this keeps you from holding your breath and adding to the internal pressure.\n\nIf your baby starts to arrive despite all your best efforts, try to ease him out gently by pushing each time you feel the urge. Once your baby's head becomes visible, gently press your hands against your perineum (the area between your vagina and anus) to keep the head from popping out too fast.\n\nDo not pull; just guide your baby out gradually. If you find the umbilical cord around your baby’s neck, hook a finger under it and slowly, gently loosen it enough to ease it over his head.\n\nOnce the head is out, gently push it slightly downward while pushing with the next urge (this should deliver the shoulders). The rest of the body should come easily after that.\n\n5. What to do once baby’s out\n\nWow, you’ve got a beautiful new baby! As soon as you’ve delivered your little one, bring him up onto your belly or chest; skin-to-skin contact will keep him warm and calm, and dry him off with a clean towel.\n\nOnce the initial fluid is wiped clean off your new baby, discard the now wet towel for a fresh, clean towel to wrap him against your body. Newborns are not great yet at regulating their body temperature, so this is an important step in keeping them warm and safe.\n\nTo help drain the amniotic fluid and stimulate first breaths, wipe baby's mouth and nose, and run your fingers from the corners of the eyes down the outsides of baby's nostrils. Then vigorously rub the sides of the back on the rib cage up and down at about the pace and pressure of washing your hair, keeping the head lower than the feet until baby starts breathing.\n\nToday, the majority of doctors don’t use an aspirator, as it's not necessary: Most babies will start to breathe on their own without any intervention or stimulation, with only 1% requiring advanced methods of resuscitation.\n\nIn the rare case that your baby is among those who need help, clear out his mouth some more with a finger, then give two quick and extremely gentle puffs of air into the mouth and nose.\n\nAfter baby is born, avoid tugging on the umbilical cord. Your uterus should expel the placenta on its own in anywhere from five to 30 minutes or more, but it's safest not to try to force it. If the placenta delivers itself, don't cut the cord (more on this below) and wait for help to arrive.\n\n6. Don’t cut or tie the umbilical cord\n\nCutting the cord yourself in a sterile fashion may be difficult if you're alone — and doing so improperly could expose your baby to infection. Not to worry — at the time of birth, about 30% of your baby’s blood is still in the placenta, which can give him two to five minutes of oxygen (this can be lifesaving if he hasn’t started breathing on his own and the EMTs haven’t arrived yet).\n\n“When the ambulance arrived [after my unplanned home birth], they clamped the cord for us and my partner cut it,” says What to Expect Community user 3beanzz. “They let me remain skin-to-skin as they helped me onto a stretcher. They were really warm people and excited for us.”\n\nSo with the cord attached, wrap the placenta in a clean towel elevated above the level of baby, if possible, and wait for the EMTs, who will cut it using sterile instruments.\n\nKEY TAKEAWAYS\n\nThe thought of experiencing an unplanned home birth can be understandably scary, but know that this is very rare: Fewer than 1% of births occur in the home, according to ACOG, and only a quarter of those are unplanned.\n\nIf you do find yourself having an unplanned birth by yourself or at home, though, the first thing to do is to call 911. Put the emergency dispatcher on speaker phone; they can help talk you through what to do next. Make sure to leave the door unlocked so the EMTs can enter easily, too.\n\nHaving an emergency birth kit is always a good idea, especially if you live in a rural area. Your kit should include clean towels, sterile gloves, sheets, clean scissors, sanitary pads, diapers, water, and instructions for infant rescue-breathing.\n\nTry your best to stay calm. And remember: Your body knows how to do this, and help is on the way.\n\nWhat to include in an emergency birth kit\n\nIf you live in an area prone to natural disasters, the nearest hospital is quite a distance away or you’re at risk of preterm labor, put together an emergency birth kit — it could come in handy in the slim chance you go into labor and can’t make it to a hospital. Your kit should include:\n\nClean towels\n\nSterile gloves\n\nSheets\n\nClean scissors\n\nSanitary pads\n\nDiapers\n\nWater\n\nInstructions for infant rescue-breathing\n\nRemember, in all likelihood you won’t have to use any part of your emergency plan — but you will be happy to have it if you need it.\n\nOther ways to be prepared for the unexpected? Give your doctor’s contact information to a few select people in case something happens and you aren’t able to make a call yourself (also, print out a copy of the information and hang it on the fridge or another prominent place in your home).\n\nBottom line: Do your best to stay calm if you find yourself in this situation, call 911 and trust your body while you wait for help to arrive.   >>     22:   "content_body": "How to Cut Back on Saying \"No!\" to Your Child\n\nby Heidi Murkoff, author of What to Expect When You're Expecting.\n\nIf you feel like you're constantly saying \"no!\" to your baby, you're not alone. Here's how to cut down on those no's while still keeping your little one from getting into trouble.\n\n\"Now that my baby's mobile, he's constantly getting into trouble. The other day he emptied the bookshelves, pulled the tablecloth off the table (and almost had a plate drop on his head), and ripped apart the magazine I was reading. I feel like I'm constantly yanking things out of his hands and saying, 'No!' What can I do to make him listen and understand?\"\n\nIt's amazing how much trouble a little mover and shaker can get into — and how quickly it can drain your patience. But while it's easy to let your little one's exploits exasperate you, there's a downside to overusing the word no. If he hears it too often, he may eventually tune you out or become hesitant to try anything new for fear of your disapproval.\n\nRemember that as babies and young toddlers, your child isn't being defiant just to bug you — exploring, experimenting and trying things his own way is how he learns about the world. So it's important to give him freedom but to also help him learn what the limits are, what's safe, and how to take responsibility for his actions.\n\nHere are some ways to cut down on those no's — and the behavior that provokes them.\n\nSet up your house for safe explorations. Create a childproof environment and you won't have to constantly stop your little one from poking, pulling and prodding at the world around him. If he just can't resist going near your collection of knickknacks or that precious crystal vase from Aunt Millie, move them out of reach for a while (you'll eventually be able to bring them back out, and at least they'll be in one piece!).\n\nOffer alternatives. Instead of a flat-out no, redirect his attention to something that's not off-limits. For example, you could say, \"You can't play with my magazine, but you can look at this one.\" Or \"You can't empty the cereal shelf, but you can take out the pots and pans.\"\n\nUse distractions. If he won't take no for an answer, physically remove him from what he's doing and get him engaged in something else. If he won't stop turning the TV on and off, for example, carry him into another room where his toys are set up and engage him in a new game. Out of sight is out of mind for a young toddler, so he's likely to be just as happy with his new activity. Another tried and true tactic: Distract your child with humor. Sometimes a totally silly face on Mom, a tickle session, or a big fat raspberry on baby's belly can make the medicine go down (and the bad behavior stop) in the most delightful way.\n\nAllow room for error. Accidents will (and should) happen — especially to little kids who need to learn from their errors. So, again, if safety's not an issue, don't make it impossible for your son to make a mistake or you'll deprive him (and yourself) of a valuable teaching moment.\n\nLet baby win…sometimes. If the stakes aren't high, let your child win the battle. An occasional victory (like being able to unravel the entire toilet paper roll) is only fair in light of all the little losses he faces every day.\n\nKeep your expectations in line. Remember, saying \"I'm sorry\" isn't a realistic expectation for an 11-month-old; however, he should be expected not to yank your hair whenever you give him a kiss.\n\nThe bottom line: Save \"no\" for rules that really matter or situations that are dangerous to your child or others. Some rules (like not pulling the cat's tail) are worth fighting for, while others (like not emptying the toy basket) may not be. That way, when you do say no your son will understand that you mean business. I hope that helps!\n\nGood luck,\n\nWhat to Expect the First Year, 3rd edition, Heidi Murkoff. Based on this, all infant life jackets should be USCG-certified and Type II PFDs. Yet whatever baby life jacket you choose, it’s crucial to always practice good water safety. \"Life jackets are not a ‘set it and forget it’ type approach,” says Natalie Livingston, CPRC, AFO, a lifeguard instructor trainer and co-founder of Alive Solutions, Inc., an educational and consulting firm focused on aquatic safety. “They do not take the place of adult supervision or of learning to swim.” The AAP recommends always being within arm’s reach of your child when in the water with them, even if they’re wearing a life jacket.\n\nExperts I spoke with also recommend:\n\nChoosing a life jacket with a grab handle, crotch strap and neck collar, as you want to easily be able to lift your little one out of the water.\n\nSticking to vivid colors, as aquatic experts prefer these to see baby better. “High visibility should be a top priority,” stresses Nelson.\n\nTesting a zipper before buying. Because getting your little one secured quickly is important, it’s best to choose a life jacket with a zipper that goes up and down easily. That, and getting out of a life jacket more quickly when back on land may avoid a meltdown.\n\nDouble-checking the weight and size of your little one. Infant life jackets are designed to fit children who weigh 33 pounds or less, per USCG standards. (The next size up is a “child” life jacket, which is made to support kids between 33 pounds and 55 pounds.)\n\nFAQs\n\nWhat type of life jacket is best for infant?\n\nThe USCG recommends that babies wear an infant Type II PFD when they are on a recreational boat. These life jackets are designed to turn the wearer’s head from a face-down position in the water into a face-up position so they can breathe. These life jackets often come in infant- and toddler-specific sizes, which is important because you should always make sure that baby’s life vest fits correctly.\n\nShould a newborn wear a life jacket?\n\nAlthough infant life jackets are designed for anyone under 30 pounds, the USCG doesn’t recommend taking infants under 18 pounds on a boat as the life vests might not fit properly. Therefore, a newborn shouldn’t wear a life jacket because it won’t be small enough and could even potentially pose a suffocation risk if it slides up and covers their mouth.\n\nDo infants need life jackets on boats?\n\nYes, the USCG recommends that babies wear a Type II infant life jacket when on a boat. However, note that this may not be until they weigh 18 pounds, or around when they turn 1 years old, because the life vest may not fit them properly yet to work correctly. But once baby is old enough for a life jacket, they should always wear one on a boat.\n\nAmerican Academy of Pediatrics, Drowning Prevention for Curious Toddlers: What Parents Need to Know, June 2023. Whether you had a vaginal birth or a C-section, your body will shed the extra tissue from pregnancy.\n\nBleeding is typically heaviest in the first week postpartum, or the first stage of lochia, before gradually lightening over time. During the second stage of lochia, you can expect pink or brown blood for roughly 12 days. In the final stage of lochia, you'll likely see spotting or a yellowish discharge for up to six weeks.\n\nDuring this time, postpartum underwear is your first line of defense. These super-comfy panties are roomy enough to hold maxi pads or ice packs for soreness; you shouldn't use tampons or menstrual cups until your doctor gives you approval, as there is a heightened risk of infection during this time.\n\nFAQs\n\nWhat type of underwear is best after giving birth?\n\nThe best postpartum underwear for you will depend on personal preference. For instance, do you prefer a compression panel? How do you feel about the environmental impact of disposables?\n\nIt will also depend on how you gave birth. New moms who had a C-section usually prefer a higher waistband, for example.\n\nFrom disposable underwear to underwear with built-in silicone pads to cover a cesarean incision, the best type of postpartum underwear will vary from person to person.\n\nHow many pairs should I buy for early postpartum?\n\nThis depends on a number of factors, including the type of postpartum underwear you’re thinking of getting. Many women find that they only need to use disposable underwear for the first week or so after giving birth, after which point they switch to regular underwear with a pad. So if you’re going the disposable route, you may find that you just need enough for a few weeks. (Assume you’ll be changing them often in the first few days.)\n\nThe quantity of non-disposables you need just depends on how frequently you want to do laundry. Even with a pad, it’s possible to experience leaks in the early days, so having a few more pairs than you think you need is always a good idea.\n\nAre disposable underwear good for postpartum?\n\nImmediately after delivery, you'll likely wear the disposable undies you're given in the hospital. In fact, docs often suggest stashing a bunch of these to take home, if you can.\n\nIf you prefer disposable mesh underwear, know that you can also buy more pairs to use at home in those first few weeks. Disposable postpartum underwear means less laundry, but it also means buying more packs.\n\nCan I wear normal underwear after a C-section?\n\nIf you’re a C-section mom, you should avoid bikini briefs (or anything that hits low) for several weeks, since most people have a surgical incision right above where their pubic hairline starts. High-waisted underwear is usually what those who had a C-section opt for, as well as underwear that has some compression or support to hold you in. There are also some pairs of postpartum underwear that have a silicone band designed to go over your incision to help prevent it from getting irritated.\n\nHow long do you need to wear postpartum underwear?\n\nThis can vary a lot from mom to mom, but most women experience their heaviest lochia, or postpartum bleeding, for the first 10 days after giving birth. After that, lochia usually transitions into lighter bleeding or spotting for four to six weeks. Postpartum underwear will probably come in handy the most during these first few weeks and months. But many moms find postpartum undies to be especially comfortable and continue wearing them beyond that point (in fact, some of the pairs on this list have rave reviews for working as “regular” underwear, too).\n\nWhat size postpartum underwear should I get?\n\nWhen shopping for postpartum underwear, you may want to order a size larger than you normally would to accommodate your postpartum body and have room for pads, particularly if the underwear is a non-postpartum style. If you’re buying underwear specifically marketed for maternity or the postpartum period, it might be safe to go with your regular size — just check the brand’s sizing chart to be sure.\n\nHow many pairs should I buy for early postpartum?\n\nThink of postpartum underwear like burp cloths — you’ll want more than you think. My advice is to have enough to keep on rotation without having to stress about doing laundry on the daily. I consider 6 to 10 pairs a general sweet spot, though it'll depend on your personal needs. As far as disposable underwear goes, make sure you have enough on hand for the first week.\n\nWhat styles work best with maxi pads or ice packs?\n\nHigh-waisted, full-coverage pairs of underwear are best. However, if you've had a C-section, be mindful of where the band sits on your incision.\n\nHow do I wash postpartum underwear safely?\n\nIt's always best to check with the brand's care instructions. In general, to keep your underwear clean and extend its lifespan, I recommend washing these on a gentle cycle with a mild detergent. Line dry when you can, otherwise, opt for low heat.\n\nWhatToExpect.com, Lochia, August 2024. WhatToExpect.com, Postpartum Symptoms, September 2021.   >>     26:   "content_body": "Here's How Fertilization Actually Works (Because Most People Don't Really Know)\n\nUpdates to copy, sources, and formatting.\n\nEgg and sperm have developed some pretty cool tricks to make conception happen. Here's what to know.\n\nYou know a baby is made when an egg meets a sperm, but there’s a lot more going on during this very cool process. In fact, it’s pretty much a miracle that one miniscule sperm will swim in the right direction and at the right time, beating out millions of other swimmers, to join forces with a lone egg and fertilize it.\n\nWhile women release just one egg each month, men release millions of sperm in a single ejaculation. But only one will reach its destination, meaning the odds are stacked against fertilization.\n\nLuckily, egg and sperm have developed some pretty cool tricks to give themselves a fighting chance. Read on to find out how fertilization actually works.\n\nKey Takeaways\n\nEgg, meet sperm. The baby-making process begins when an egg and sperm join to create a fertilized egg known as a zygote.\n\nFind your fertile window. Your timing has to be precise for fertilization to occur — sperm can live up to five days but an egg has a lifespan of just 12 to 24 hours.\n\nIt's a wild ride! It's amazing that millions of sperm zoom through your vagina but only one can claim the prized egg that later implants and starts the pregnancy.\n\nWhat is fertilization?\n\nFertilization is when a man's sperm combines with a woman's egg to form a single cell. It’s one of the first steps toward pregnancy, but there are more hurdles to cross. Trusted SourceCleveland ClinicConceptionSee All Sources [1]\n\nWant to know more about your fertile window as you try to conceive? Download the What to Expect app for your go-to-guide to all things baby-making.\n\nWhere does fertilization occur?\n\nIt's a common misconception that fertilization happens in the uterus, since that's where the baby develops. But fertilization actually occurs in the fallopian tubes.\n\nEach sperm has a single goal: to meet up with the egg. To reach the target, though, a sperm cell has to go on a lengthy and strenuous journey.\n\nFirst, it must make its way from the vagina to the cervix, and then it has to swim through the uterus to the fallopian tubes. Once there, if the sperm is the lucky one, it will penetrate the egg and fertilize it. The newly fertilized egg (now called a zygote) will make its way from the fallopian tubes to the uterus with the help of small finger-like structures called fimbriae. Once there, it implants in the uterine wall and continues to develop into your baby.\n\nMost of the time, implantation occurs in the uterus as it should. However, sometimes the fertilized egg implants and grows somewhere outside of the uterus. This is called an ectopic pregnancy.\n\nUsually, an ectopic pregnancy occurs in a fallopian tube (which is why you may have heard of it being called a tubal pregnancy), but it may also happen in an ovary, the cervix or even the abdomen.\n\nSince none of those areas has the right tissue or the space to accommodate a growing pregnancy, an ectopic pregnancy is not a viable pregnancy.\n\nWhen does fertilization occur?\n\nFor fertilization to happen, the timing and conditions must be just right. The fertilization process can only occur during a fairly small window within just a few days of ovulation (a few days before up until a day after you ovulate).\n\nEven if a sperm does make its way to the fallopian tube, that doesn’t mean it will definitely be able to fertilize the egg. Aside from various fertility-related problems that can hamper the process, the timing may be off, meaning the sperm arrived too early or too late to meet up with the egg. Or the sperm may have entered the wrong fallopian tube (an egg is usually present in only one of the fallopian tubes in any given month).\n\nHow long does it take for a sperm to fertilize an egg?\n\nSperm are super-fast swimmers and can reach the egg in about an hour, while the entire fertilization process can take several hours. Contrary to what many people believe, fertilization doesn’t occur immediately after sex.\n\nFor about half an hour after sex, the semen coagulates in the vagina, forming a physical barrier that prevents the sperm from wandering very far in the wrong direction. This protection disappears within 30 minutes when the semen (at first gel-like) liquifies. Trusted SourceUCSF HealthConception: How It WorksSee All Sources [2]\n\nAny sperm that haven't made it up through the cervix by then are eliminated from the running by the vagina’s natural acidity, which destroys any errant cells, including sperm.\n\nThe sperm that make it to the next step — the cervical canal — spend time going through biochemical changes, picking up the tail-thrashing speed that's required for them to swim their way through the uterus and fallopian tubes to find the egg.\n\nThe cervical canal is a much more welcoming environment, where the mucus is specially designed to transport sperm efficiently when you're most fertile.\n\nAs you approach ovulation, your suddenly copious mucus becomes stretchy, clear, and thin (that's one of the reasons why observing it is such an effective method for tracking ovulation). The changes happen on a microscopic level as well, as strings of molecules line up like train tracks so that sperm can hop on and ride to their destination.\n\nThe sperm that do reach the egg still have their work cut out for them. The race is on to be the first one to plow through the hard outer layer.\n\nAnd there's plenty of competition. Hundreds of sperm will surround the egg during the frantic battle to the finish, all trying to penetrate the egg's membrane to reach the cytoplasm, where the sperm will then release its own genetic contribution.\n\nAs soon as one lucky sperm cell succeeds in penetrating the egg, the egg immediately undergoes a chemical reaction that prevents other sperm cells from following suit. Then the chromosomes carried by the sperm and egg come together, and the egg is officially fertilized.\n\nCan you feel when an egg gets fertilized?\n\nNo, you won't feel when an egg gets fertilized. You also won’t feel pregnant after two or three days. But some women can feel implantation, the process in which the fertilized egg travels down the fallopian tube and buries itself deep within the wall of the uterus.\n\nThis happens about eight to nine days after fertilization, though it can happen earlier or later. Symptoms of implantation may include abdominal cramps and light bleeding. Whether you feel anything or not, implantation is the moment that fertilization gives way to pregnancy!\n\nHow long can sperm live inside you?\n\nSperm can survive inside the female reproductive tract for about 72 hours. And, in some cases, the sperm can live for up to five days. But the lifespan of an egg is much shorter. The egg lives for only 12 to 24 hours after ovulation.\n\nIf sperm aren't hanging around by time the egg makes it to the fallopian tube (or if they don't reach the destination shortly after the egg arrives), the body reabsorbs the egg and the window of opportunity for conception that month closes.\n\nAs you've no doubt learned by now, the road to fertilization is a bumpy one, with plenty of twists and turns. It takes the right conditions and perfect timing for the egg and sperm to meet up and produce that baby you're hoping for. But once they do, you've embarked on your own amazing journey: the journey of motherhood.",

We selected a variety of strollers to suit different family sizes.\n\nLocation : Families living in urban areas may appreciate a narrower stroller with strong maneuverability to help navigate small doorways and busy streets. And nothing is more convenient than a travel system. These car seat-stroller combos make getting from point A to point B with your little one so much easier.\n\nA travel system is basically a full-size stroller and a compatible infant car seat that clips into the stroller when you're on foot or into the car when you're on (big) wheels. Car seat-stroller combos let you travel with your baby for years — I have been able to use mine from infancy right up through toddlerhood.\n\nMost families need both a stroller and an infant car seat when they have a newborn. And in my experience as a mom of two, making sure the two products are compatible increases how much use you get out of both. Picture this: You’re driving with your baby in the backseat and need to stop to run a quick errand. Because you have a travel system stroller, you don’t have to unbuckle and lift your baby out of her car seat then re-buckle her into the stroller (possibly waking her up in the process). Instead, you simply unclip the entire car seat from its base and attach it to the stroller frame.\n\nNot to mention, I’ve found that travel systems let you knock two big items off your baby checklist in one go and often allow you to save some money.\n\nHow We Chose the Best Travel Systems\n\nTo find the best travel systems, I compiled a list of around 50 car seat and stroller sets currently on the market. Parents say the Evenflo Pivot Modular Travel System represents excellent value, thanks to an easy-to-use stroller and included top-of-the-line car seat.\n\nA highlight of the Evenflo Pivot is the impressive six modes of use, which offer tons of versatility for parents to configure the seats front- or rear-facing, depending on preferences. This functionality is available for the infant car seat, toddler seat and newborn bassinet. (The latter is notable, as most strollers don’t let you change the position of the newborn bassinet.) It’s relatively lightweight and easy to switch between the different modes, parents say.\n\nPlus, many parents also note how nice it feels to handle and use, so you don’t have to sacrifice convenience for price. And there are a number of nice-to-have features you don’t always find on more affordable brands of car seats and strollers, such as a parent cup holder, bumper with snack tray and a large undercarriage storage basket. Clipping in the infant car seat is also a breeze.\n\nThe only downside: Some parents say that the stroller that comes with this travel system doesn’t have the best maneuverability and can be tricky to turn on certain surfaces.\n\nCommunity Reviews\n\nkas1990 “I got the Evenflo Pivot, about $300. It's a car seat, a stroller and a bassinet that converts to a toddler seat. Long lasting and definitely worth the money.”\n\nbwnapier “After doing some pretty extensive research, we will be getting the Evenflo Pivot! Super affordable and highly rated.”\n\nBest Travel System for Multiples\n\nEvenflo Pivot Xpand Modular Travel System with SafeMax Infant Car Seat\n\nHas 22 possible configurations and can grow to accommodate three kids\n\nSome reviewers say it doesn’t feel as high-end as other models\n\nStroller Specs: Weight: 28.6 lbs. Dimensions: ‎34 x 26.5 x 41.5 inches Weight Limit: Up to 55 lbs.\n\nCar Seat Specs: Weight: 7.6 lbs. Weight/Height Limit: 4 lbs. to 35 lbs.\n\nWhy We Love It\n\nTraveling with one baby is hard enough, but two? You need some truly special gear for that. Enter the Evenflo Pivot Xpand Modular Travel System: This multiple-friendly stroller-car seat combo includes the brand’s full-size Pivot Xpand stroller with the SafeMax Infant Car Seat. It has an impressive number of possible configurations, and for parents of twins or two under 2, it’s a must-have.\n\nThere are 22 different ways you can set up the seats, depending on whether you’re using SafeMax Infant Car Seat and/or the included toddler seat. As a result, you can use this same stroller/car seat combo (with the addition of a second seat and/or riderboard) to push up to three children until the toddler years. For less than $500, that’s an incredible value.\n\nSize aside, What to Expect parents appreciate the Evenflo Pivot Xpand Modular’s impressive list of features, including self-standing fold, front wheel swivel, peekaboo canopy, adjustable handle and a surprisingly roomy basket. Another bonus is that there are no tools or extra parts needed to convert the stroller from a single to a double. Reviewers find that it’s easy to install and a breeze to push.\n\nSome reviewers do say that the stroller doesn’t feel like it’s made with as high-quality materials as others on the market. If having a luxury travel system is important to you, you might prefer one of the other options on this list.\n\nCommunity Reviews\n\nscotiamama \"We’re going with the Evenflo Pivot Xpand. My daughter is 1.5 now, but still loves being in the stroller when we go for walks. I have the regular Pivot, and I like it! Plus, it’s affordable.\"\n\nWhat to Look for in a Travel System\n\nThe best travel system consists of a stroller and car seat that are not only compatible with each other, but with your family’s lifestyle, too. Because every family has different needs, here’s what you might keep in mind when shopping:\n\nSize: This includes both a stroller’s dimensions as well as how many children it can accommodate. For example, some parents may prefer a larger stroller with a smoother ride, while others (particularly those who live in cities where they’re often navigating narrow streets) might appreciate a slimmer stroller frame.\n\nVersatility: It’s often worth investing in a stroller that can adapt to changing situations. For example, if you have twins, you’ll need a travel system stroller that can handle more than one baby at a time in two infant car seats. You might also prefer for the travel system to include a convertible stroller that can become a double in the future should you have another baby. Some families might also like a travel system with a reversible stroller that lets them face baby forward or backwards.\n\nManeuverability: The easier it is to push and pull a stroller, the more likely you are to use it often. You’ll want a stroller that moves smoothly and turns without issue, even making tight corners.\n\nExtra features: Some travel system strollers are basic, and focused on getting baby from point A to point B; others have additional features, like cup holders on the car seat, an adjustable stroller handlebar and washable fabrics. If you tend to tote a lot of gear with you, you’ll also want to look for a travel system stroller that can handle your stuff, too, such as one with parent storage or a large under-carriage basket.\n\nFAQs\n\nShould I get a car seat stroller combo?\n\nThis is a personal decision that really depends on your family’s needs. A travel system stroller allows you to switch your baby from car to stroller easily, but it might not be right for everyone.\n\nA travel system can come in handy for families who are often out of the house. Because you already have the car seat installed, you only need to remember the stroller frame. A travel system can also help you save money: buying a car seat and stroller as a set may be cheaper than purchasing them separately. Still, there are some downsides to keep in mind before you invest:\n\nThe car seats that come in travel system strollers are for infants only, so you'll need to invest in a compatible toddler car seat later.\n\nEven the lightest travel system stroller can be bulky, making it tough to load into and out of your trunk.\n\nInfant stroller travel systems may not be good for dirt and gravel roads, since they're heavier than most strollers and tougher to push on uneven surfaces. They can also be tight squeezes through narrower grocery-store aisles.\n\nYou can only use the car seat that comes with the stroller (and not all companies sell extra car seat bases separately from the travel system). So if you have more than one car, you'll need to buy a second car seat if you don't want to unhook and reattach the one base the stroller comes with.\n\nIs a car seat/stroller combo safe?\n\nCar seat/stroller combos are very safe as long as they meet safety guidelines.\n\nWhen buying any car seat (regardless of whether or not it’s part of a travel system), always make sure the product you’re considering:\n\nIsn’t too old (you can check with the manufacturer or look for a label with the date it was made). Make sure, too, it has a label with the date of manufacture and model number.\n\nDoesn’t have any visible cracks in it.\n\nComes with instructions so you can safely install the seat.\n\nIsn’t missing any parts.\n\nWasn’t recalled (if you’re unsure, you can contact the NHTSA Vehicle Safety Hotline at 888/327-4236 or visit their website ).\n\nHasn’t been in a car crash.\n\nStrollers should have:\n\nEasy-to-operate brakes that lock two wheels instead of just one to provide an extra measure of safety.\n\nA wide base that can’t easily be tipped over.\n\nA five-point harness with straps over both shoulders, hips and between the legs.\n\nOne footrest that extends footrest all the way across both sitting areas (for a side-by-side double stroller).\n\nOnce you’ve purchased a travel system, take these steps to ensure that your little one's secure:\n\nAs you put the system together, be sure to include all the pieces. There may be a lot of them, but every last one has a purpose.\n\nPractice clipping the car seat into the stroller and unclipping it again before your baby's sitting in it (so you're a pro before you add a wee wiggler to the mix). Once your baby's in the car seat, gently shake the handle to make sure the seat's fully attached to the stroller before you hit the road.\n\nLook for a label that reads \"This restraint system conforms to all applicable federal motor vehicle safety standards. This restraint is certified for use in all motor vehicles and aircraft.\" This label means the seat has passed rigorous federal safety standards.\n\nAs always, remember that infant car seats should not be used for routine sleep, according to the AAP. The safest sleep position for a baby is flat on her back.\n\nWhat are the different types of travel system strollers?\n\nAt their core, travel system strollers have a few things in common: They allow you to nestle baby’s car seat right inside and wheel away. But there are a few different types out there:\n\nOne-piece travel system strollers. These convert the car seat into the stroller versus having a separate stroller.\n\nTwo-piece travel system strollers. Most stroller systems are designed this way, with a separate car seat and stroller that work together.\n\nAdjustable travel system strollers. These stroller systems allow you to change the height for your comfort — and baby’s.\n\nTwo-seat travel system strollers. While many travel stroller systems are designed for one car seat, some can fit two to accommodate twins.\n\nAmerican Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), How to Keep Your Sleeping Baby Safe: AAP Policy Explained, July 2022.
